definition: Diverge means to move or develop apart in different directions.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word diverge. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know diverge should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The sisters' accents began to diverge the year one moved to Glasgow, until strangers no longer took them for family on the phone.
Drift is the gentlest pulling apart — two boats drift apart on a current without either changing course — and it stops short of diverge.
Split goes further than diverge: diverging paths still run on within sight of each other, while a split is a clean break into separate pieces.

Branch describes the moment one line splits the way a tree limb does — a road forks, a river parts, and both arms keep growing from the same trunk. Diverge is about what follows: two things moving or developing further apart over time. A trail branches in a second; the two paths then diverge for miles.

Splinter means breaking into smaller pieces or factions, often suddenly and with force — a committee splinters into rival camps. Diverge is slower and gentler: each thing stays whole while the two of them move apart in different directions. A party that splinters shatters; two parties that diverge simply grow separate.

Two food carts opened the same spring, run by cousins using one shared dumpling recipe.
Within ten years the menus had nothing in common: one cart went fiery Sichuan, the other folded in Polish fillings from the neighborhood.
Regulars watched the two kitchens diverge a little further every season.
Diverge is more exact than 'differ' because it means to move or develop apart — it is a verb of motion, and it needs time or distance to happen in.
Two menus simply differ on the day you compare them; they diverge over the years that pull them apart.
Diverge is the working verb of science and planning for things that move apart over time — paths, populations, forecasts, versions.
Where there is no motion, plain differ is better; where the break is sudden and final, split.
Its opposite number is converge, the same lean bending together instead of apart.

The twin apprentices left the same Murano workshop in 1962 carrying identical toolkits and identical habits.
One settled in Vienna, the other in Osaka, and for a decade their goblets could be swapped without anyone noticing.
Then the two practices began to diverge: Vienna's stems grew architectural and severe, while Osaka's softened into seaweed curves.
Neither brother quarreled with the other or with Murano; each simply followed his adopted city's light.
By 1990 collectors could date and place a piece at a glance, so far apart had the two styles traveled.
